precepts.text: Be thou for the people to God-ward, that thou mayest bring the causes unto God. That is what Job was doing when men gave ear and waited at his counsel.
precepts.point: If I laughed on them, they believed it not: Job had an austere spirit. I chose out their way: he counseled and directed them. And sat chief, and dwelt as a king in the army, as one that comforteth the mourners. Job sat like a king in the army.

note.label: Job Sees America's 250th Anniversary

precepts.why:
“My glory was fresh in me, and my bow was renewed in my hand. Unto me men gave ear, and waited, and kept silence at my counsel.” Job was up there. He was no pushover, no punk.

This is what Jethro told Moses: “Hearken now unto my voice, I will give thee counsel, and God shall be with thee: Be thou for the people to God-ward, that thou mayest bring the causes unto God”.

That is what Job was doing. He was for the people to God-ward, bringing their causes to God, and men waited in silence for his counsel. “After my words they spake not again”: after Job spoke, you had nothing to say. “I chose out their way, and sat chief”: he counseled them and directed them, and dwelt as a king in the army.

precepts.text: The priest of Midian gave Moses Zipporah his daughter, and she bare Gershom; Reuel is Jethro, and the daughters took Moses for an Egyptian.
precepts.point: Jethro was not an Israelite; he and his kindred were not of the tribes.

note.label: Exodus 18: Jethro's Counsel and Righteous Leadership

precepts.why:
Jethro, “the priest of Midian, Moses’ father in law”, heard all that God had done for Moses and for Israel, and came to Moses in the wilderness with Zipporah and her two sons, Gershom and Eliezer. Exodus 2 shows who this man is. “Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters”, and when the shepherds drove them from the troughs, “Moses stood up and helped them, and watered their flock.” When the daughters came home their father is named: “And when they came to Reuel their father”. He sent for Moses to eat bread, “And Moses was content to dwell with the man: and he gave Moses Zipporah his daughter.” She bare him a son, “and he called his name Gershom: for he said, I have been a stranger in a strange land.”

That is the same wife and the same son named here in Exodus 18: Zipporah, and Gershom, of whom Moses said “I have been an alien in a strange land”. So the priest of Midian who gave Moses Zipporah in Exodus 2 is the priest of Midian who comes to him at the mount of God in Exodus 18. Reuel and Jethro are one person.

Exodus 2 also holds one of the color scriptures. The daughters told their father, “An Egyptian delivered us out of the hand of the shepherds”. Moses was an Israelite, but he was taken for an Egyptian, because Israel looked like the Egyptians.

And Jethro was not an Israelite. He and his kindred were not of the tribes.

precepts.text: All the gods of the nations are idols, but the Lord made the heavens; give unto the Lord the glory due unto his name.
precepts.point: Nebuchadnezzar came to praise and extol and honour the King of heaven, for those that walk in pride he is able to abase. The heathen understand that the Most High is greater than all other gods; it is our people that want a god that does not look like them.

note.label: Exodus 18: Jethro's Counsel and Righteous Leadership

precepts.why:
Jethro rejoiced for all the goodness the Lord had done to Israel and confessed, “Now I know that the Lord is greater than all gods: for in the thing wherein they dealt proudly he was above them.” The psalm says the same of every god Jethro measured the Lord against: “For all the gods of the nations are idols: but the Lord made the heavens.”

Then it calls the nations to do what Jethro did: “Give unto the Lord, O ye kindreds of the people, give unto the Lord glory and strength. Give unto the Lord the glory due unto his name: bring an offering, and come into his courts.” Jethro, a priest of Midian and not an Israelite, gave the Lord that glory: “Blessed be the Lord, who hath delivered you out of the hand of the Egyptians, and out of the hand of Pharaoh”. Other non-Israelites came to that same knowledge.

precepts.text: Naaman, captain of the host of Syria, was a mighty man in valour, but he was a leper.
precepts.point: Nebuchadnezzar came to praise and extol and honour the King of heaven, for those that walk in pride he is able to abase. The heathen understand that the Most High is greater than all other gods; it is our people that want a god that does not look like them.

note.label: Exodus 18: Jethro's Counsel and Righteous Leadership

precepts.why:
Naaman is another non-Israelite who came to know what Jethro knew. He was “captain of the host of the king of Syria”, “a great man with his master, and honourable, because by him the Lord had given deliverance unto Syria: he was also a mighty man in valour, but he was a leper.”

A great man of another nation, honourable and mighty in valour, and yet a leper. That is who the Lord was about to heal, and who would confess, like Jethro, that the Lord is greater than all gods.

precepts.text: Naaman dipped seven times in Jordan and was clean, and confessed there is no God in all the earth but in Israel; a heathen vowed to sacrifice to no other god but the Lord.
precepts.point: Nebuchadnezzar came to praise and extol and honour the King of heaven, for those that walk in pride he is able to abase. The heathen understand that the Most High is greater than all other gods; it is our people that want a god that does not look like them.

note.label: Exodus 18: Jethro's Counsel and Righteous Leadership

precepts.why:
Naaman “went he down, and dipped himself seven times in Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God: and his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child, and he was clean.” Then he came back and stood before the man of God and said, “Behold, now I know that there is no God in all the earth, but in Israel”. Those are Jethro’s words: now I know. A Syrian, healed of his leprosy in Jordan, confessed that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel.

His faith was so strong he asked for “two mules’ burden of earth”, “for thy servant will henceforth offer neither burnt offering nor sacrifice unto other gods, but unto the Lord.” A heathen vowed to sacrifice to no other god but the Lord.

He even asked pardon for bowing in the house of Rimmon with his master: “when my master goeth into the house of Rimmon to worship there, and he leaneth on my hand, and I bow myself in the house of Rimmon: when I bow down myself in the house of Rimmon, the Lord pardon thy servant in this thing.” He knew that bowing there, only because his master leaned on his hand, was a thing to ask pardon for. That is how far a non-Israelite went once he knew the Lord is greater than all gods.

precepts.text: Nebuchadnezzar praised and extolled the King of heaven, whose works are truth, and those that walk in pride he is able to abase.
precepts.point: Nebuchadnezzar came to praise and extol and honour the King of heaven, for those that walk in pride he is able to abase. The heathen understand that the Most High is greater than all other gods; it is our people that want a god that does not look like them.

note.label: Exodus 18: Jethro's Counsel and Righteous Leadership

precepts.why:
Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon, came to the same confession: “Now I Nebuchadnezzar praise and extol and honour the King of heaven, all whose works are truth, and his ways judgment: and those that walk in pride he is able to abase.”

That is exactly what Jethro saw in Egypt: “in the thing wherein they dealt proudly he was above them.” The Egyptians walked in pride and the Lord abased them, and Nebuchadnezzar learned that those that walk in pride he is able to abase.

Jethro, Naaman and Nebuchadnezzar: the heathen understand that the Most High is greater than all other gods. It is our people that want a god that does not look like them.

precepts.text: The scribes and the Pharisees sit in Moses' seat; observe what they bid, but do not after their works.
precepts.point: The scribes and the Pharisees sat in Moses' seat, which is why their words were to be observed but their works not followed, for they say and do not.

note.label: Exodus 18: Jethro's Counsel and Righteous Leadership

precepts.why:
Moses told Jethro why the people stood before him from morning to evening: “the people come unto me to enquire of God: When they have a matter, they come unto me; and I judge between one and another, and I do make them know the statutes of God, and his laws.” That responsibility, judging the people and making them know the statutes of God, is Moses’ seat.

Christ speaks of that seat: “The scribes and the Pharisees sit in Moses’ seat”. They sat where Moses sat, judging and giving the people the law. That is why he said, “All therefore whatsoever they bid you observe, that observe and do; but do not ye after their works: for they say, and do not.” Their words were to be observed because they came from Moses’ seat; their works were not to be followed, for they say and do not.

precepts.text: Captains over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens, and officers among the tribes, charged to judge righteously and not respect persons, for the judgment is God's.
precepts.point: Judgment did not pass away with the Old Testament. He that is spiritual judgeth all things, and the spiritual man is the man that keeps the commandments. The saints shall judge the world, so brethren should judge the smallest matters among themselves instead of going to law before the unjust; only matters of life and death under today's system go outside.

note.label: Exodus 18: Jethro's Counsel and Righteous Leadership

precepts.why:
Moses recounts how Jethro’s counsel was put in place: “So I took the chief of your tribes, wise men, and known, and made them heads over you, captains over thousands, and captains over hundreds, and captains over fifties, and captains over tens, and officers among your tribes.” These are the rulers of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens. This is the structure of righteous leadership the Most High established: captains and officers over the tribes, offices never heard in the church.

Then the charge to the judges: “Hear the causes between your brethren, and judge righteously between every man and his brother, and the stranger that is with him. Ye shall not respect persons in judgment; but ye shall hear the small as well as the great; ye shall not be afraid of the face of man; for the judgment is God’s”. The men set over the people had to be such as fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness, because the judgment they gave was God’s.

Then the hard cases: “the cause that is too hard for you, bring it unto me, and I will hear it.” That is the order Jethro gave: every great matter to Moses, every small matter judged by the rulers. It is the same today. The hard matters go to the high-ranking officers and ultimately the bishop, while the smaller matters are judged by the lower-ranking officers.

precepts.text: He that is spiritual judgeth all things; the spiritual man keeps the commandments.
precepts.point: Judgment did not pass away with the Old Testament. He that is spiritual judgeth all things, and the spiritual man is the man that keeps the commandments. The saints shall judge the world, so brethren should judge the smallest matters among themselves instead of going to law before the unjust; only matters of life and death under today's system go outside.

note.label: Exodus 18: Jethro's Counsel and Righteous Leadership

precepts.why:
Judgment did not pass away with the Old Testament. Paul writes, “But he that is spiritual judgeth all things, yet he himself is judged of no man.” The spiritual man is the man that keeps the commandments.

That is who Jethro told Moses to look for: able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness. Men like that are spiritual, and the spiritual man judges. The rulers of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens were to judge the people at all seasons, and he that is spiritual still judgeth all things.

precepts.text: The saints shall judge the world; do not go to law before the unjust when you are able to judge the smallest matters.
precepts.point: Judgment did not pass away with the Old Testament. He that is spiritual judgeth all things, and the spiritual man is the man that keeps the commandments. The saints shall judge the world, so brethren should judge the smallest matters among themselves instead of going to law before the unjust; only matters of life and death under today's system go outside.

note.label: Exodus 18: Jethro's Counsel and Righteous Leadership

precepts.why:
“Dare any of you, having a matter against another, go to law before the unjust, and not before the saints? Do ye not know that the saints shall judge the world? and if the world shall be judged by you, are ye unworthy to judge the smallest matters?”

That is the very order of Exodus 18: every small matter they shall judge. The saints shall judge the world, so brethren are not unworthy to judge the smallest matters among themselves, and they should, instead of going to law before the unjust. Only matters of life and death under today’s system go outside.

precepts.text: The thing that thou doest is not good; thou wilt surely wear away, both thou and this people, for the thing is too heavy for one man.
precepts.point: His father in law told him the thing was not good: judging alone would wear away both Moses and the people. The counsel was to provide able men that fear God and set them in ranks over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens.

note.label: Deuteronomy 1: The Second Giving of the Law

precepts.why:
When Moses says “I am not able to bear you myself alone”, he is referring back to what his father in law saw in Exodus 18. Moses sat judging the people alone from morning until evening, the people waiting all day in line, because they came to him to inquire of God and to be shown the statutes and laws. His father in law told him: “The thing that thou doest is not good. Thou wilt surely wear away, both thou, and this people that is with thee: for this thing is too heavy for thee; thou art not able to perform it thyself alone.”

The Lord had multiplied Israel “as the stars of heaven for multitude”, and every one of them came with cumbrance, burden, and strife. One man judging all of that would wear away, and the people waiting on him would wear away with him. That is what Moses is asking: “How can I myself alone bear your cumbrance, and your burden, and your strife?” The thing was too heavy for one man; it was not good, and it had to change.

precepts.text: Provide able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness, and place them as rulers of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens.
precepts.point: His father in law told him the thing was not good: judging alone would wear away both Moses and the people. The counsel was to provide able men that fear God and set them in ranks over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens.

note.label: Deuteronomy 1: The Second Giving of the Law

precepts.why:
The counsel of Moses' father in law was not only that the load was too heavy, but what to do about it: “Moreover thou shalt provide out of all the people able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, and rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens”. Able men that fear God, set in ranks over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens, so the burden Moses could not bear alone was shared.

That is the answer to “How can I myself alone bear your cumbrance, and your burden, and your strife?” A people as the stars of heaven for multitude needs rulers over them, and they had to be a particular kind of men: fearing God, men of truth, hating covetousness. Moses is reminding Israel that the order set among them came from that counsel.

precepts.text: Teach them the ordinances and laws and show them the way wherein they must walk.
precepts.point: The way we must walk is defined by the ordinances and laws we are taught.

note.label: 2 Chronicles 17: Jehoshaphat Sends Teachers Through the Cities

precepts.why:
“And thou shalt teach them ordinances and laws, and shalt shew them the way wherein they must walk, and the work that they must do.”

The way we must walk is defined by the ordinances and laws we are taught. Jehoshaphat walked that way: he “sought to the Lord God of his father, and walked in his commandments, and not after the doings of Israel.”

precepts.point: Habakkuk 2:4 says the just shall live by his faith, meaning the justified seed of Israel shall live by faith in Christ rather than by animal sacrifice.

note.label: Galatians 2: The Council at Jerusalem and Justification by Faith

precepts.why:
“And thou shalt teach them ordinances and laws, and shalt shew them the way wherein they must walk, and the work that they must do.”

The work they must do is the ordinances and the laws. Works, in scripture, are the keeping of what the Lord commands. The works of the law by which no flesh is justified are the works of the sacrificial law; the way wherein we must walk, the commandments, is still the work we must do.
